set.p: The scene is laid in Modern Babylon, Capital of the Island of Tempestorn.

div.head: SCENE I.
div.stage: Enter three hungry Mechanics, pursuing a lean dog with a beef bone.

sp.speaker: 1st. Mec.
sp.p: I have him! I have him!

sp.speaker: 2nd. Mec.
sp.p: Yes, but have you got the bone?

sp.speaker: 3rd. Mec.
sp.p: Aye—the bone.

sp.speaker: 1st. Mec.
sp.p: Yes, to be sure; leave me alone for that.

sp.speaker: 2nd. Mec.
sp.p: Troth, and I've no objection to leave you alone with it, for there is no meat upon it.

sp.speaker: 3rd. Mec.
sp.p: This bone is the emblem of our hopes. We envied, and pursued, and panted after the poor possessor, eager to seize—imagining a meal—and here ends the chase. We hunted what we thought a prize—and it was one, while we fancied it; but no sooner have we seized upon it, than the fat game of hope changes to disappointment; which is hope's reality all the world over.

sp.speaker: 2nd. Mec.
sp.p: O, you've been hearing Robert Vision speak?

sp.speaker: 3rd. Mec.
sp.p: Yes, he makes one think.

sp.speaker: 2nd. Mec.
sp.p: Could'nt you have cut the matter shorter, by saying the beef bone was an emblem— the only one remaining—of the roast beef of old Tempestorn?

sp.speaker: 1st. Mec.
sp.p: Hark ye, old chap, if Robert Vision makes you think, s'pose you tell us what you think of him?

sp.speaker: 3rd. Mec.
sp.p: Why, I think he often does much the same that we are apt to do at the public-house; reckons without his host.

div.stage: Enter a Bricklayer and a Mason.

sp.speaker: 1st. Mec.
sp.p: You are a Visionite, too; what do you think of Robert?

sp.speaker: Brick.
sp.p: Why, I think his buildings would be the finest things in nature, only he uses no mortar.

sp.speaker: 3rd. Mec.
sp.p: Then the first strong wind that comes floors it, of course.

sp.speaker: Mason.
sp.p: I've heard him speak, and like him much; his promises, and his purposes too, are the right sort of things for all men. But when I've gone away and considered his plans over to myself, it always seemed to me that he placed the first stone well enough, as a small beginning, and then left it and went to place another a mile off, and so on in that way. Now, if he would only place the second stone upon the first, and not the third until those two were fixed, and made inseparable, there would be some chance for the working classes.

sp.speaker: 1st. Mec.
sp.p: Ah! I see if we don't help ourselves, nobody else can; that's the long and the short of it.

div.stage: Enter Fat Jaques, followed by a crowd of ragged Manufacturers and other Relatives.

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: I can't get any employment myself, except I work without being paid for it; a very general complaint now-a-days. I find it difficult to get cotton or wool, and difficult to get a market for it; whether in the shape of an old woman's shawl, a Bishop's breeches, or a coverlid for the horses of a nobleman's carriage; I find it difficult to get the raw material; difficult to work it up, and get any folks to buy it; and impossible to get my money if they do. I've a great mind to hang myself— and I would too, only I'm so hungry.

sp.speaker: 2nd. Mec.
sp.p: O, for the matter of that, as you're never likely to be better off, you need'nt wait. But you're always hungry. I never knew you otherwise.

sp.speaker: Mason.
sp.p: Well, and why shouldn't he have enough food?
You work hard for it, why shouldn't you have it?

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: Now that's just what I say; why shouldn't I? And I've said this for many years. All these manufacturers say the same. I've just paid them twopence a head all round, for their day's labour, working as hard myself as any of them. They say it isn't anything like enough to keep body and soul together, wives and children included. There's no doubt of this; no need for the women to ding it in my ears so incessantly. Hunger makes our women turn politicians; that alone shows the state of the country. But what can I do? I pay the utmost I can on all possible occasions?

sp.speaker: Manufacturers, &c.
sp.p: So you do—so you do —you are an old fool for it, daddy.

sp.speaker: 1st. Mec.
sp.p: You squander your money on all sorts of humbugs.

sp.speaker: 2nd. Mec.
sp.p: You let any hoax in the shape of a cocked-hat or a roll of parchment with the arms upon it, tap you to the last drop.

sp.speaker: Manufac.
sp.p: You do—you do—you are an unfair tapster yourself; you give us the iron hoops off the butts, and our oppressors the beer.

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: Come, I say.

sp.speaker: 2nd. Mec.
sp.p: Your size is still like a butt, and it would take the largest hoops to compass you; yet they only surround emptiness, and your spirit is like the rust upon them.

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: But I say, though!—

sp.speaker: 3rd. Mec.
sp.p: Friend, you are neither a reasonable, nor a brave man.

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: I'll soon show you—I do say—

sp.speaker: Mason.
sp.p: You are extravagant, but not just; you are without discrimination or spirit.

sp.speaker: Brick.
sp.p: You ought to have sense beat into your head with a brick-bat.

sp.speaker: Manufac.
sp.p: So he ought; let's beat some in; there's no other way, to a certainty.

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: I won't have any more of it; I've been worked, and baited, and beat and badgered enough, these many years, and I'll bear it no longer. D---, and dumb-founder, and be hanged to all the lords and ladies, and crowned kickshaws, and jews, and pharisees, and vandals of the island! aye, and of the earth too! I won't put up with it any longer!

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.p: Ha! ha! ha! Bravo, Jaques! bravo!

sp.speaker: 3rd. Mec.
sp.p: My good man, you've said that a great many times before.

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.p: He has—to be sure he has!

sp.speaker: 2nd. Mec.
sp.p: O, you're a natural beast of burden.

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: It a'nt my nature to be told so!

sp.speaker: Brick.
sp.p: It's quite true, though.

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: It's a lie!

sp.speaker: Manufac.
sp.p: You know it's true.

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: You are a swinish multitude!
sp.stage: (they knock Fat Jaques down—a scuffle ensues).
sp.p: —The Lord Mayor's coach is coming! the Lord Mayor's coach!

div.stage: Enter Cockney (servant to Jaques), running breathless.

sp.speaker: Cockney.
sp.p: Oh! Mr. Fat Jaques—here, sir, please, sir—here's the cockt-hat show!

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: Where! where! which way?

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.p: There it is! there it is!

div.head: SCENE II.
div.stage: Enter Lord Mayor's Coach, with Procession, &c, followed by motley groups. Music.

sp.speaker: Constable.
sp.p: Stand aside, you young dog, you!

sp.speaker: Young Dog.
sp.p: I sha'nt. Vot d'ye think o' that now?

div.stage: Enter Fat Jaques and Cockney running at the head of a crowd.

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: Where is it? oh! here's the coach!

sp.speaker: A Mec.
sp.p: Get off my toes, will you?

sp.speaker: A Countryman.
sp.p: I can't, master; there's no room to set a foot elsewhere.

sp.speaker: Cockney.
sp.p: My eye! what a beauty! it's all fresh golded! I say, sir, isn't it a beauty?

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: I never saw it look so well before.

sp.speaker: Apprentice.
sp.p: How werry 'ansome!

sp.speaker: A Lawyer's Clerk.
sp.p: I wish I could get near enough to lay my hand on it.

sp.speaker: A Young Thief.
sp.p: So does I, too.

sp.speaker: A Voice.
sp.p: Is that the Lord Mayor? Which is the Lord Mayor? Is that chain round his neck all real gold?

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: To be sure it is—of course.

sp.speaker: A Shop-keeper.
sp.p: How I like to see 'em go along so. I never saw a finer sight.

sp.speaker: 2nd. Shop.
sp.p: Capital well that fellow plays the trumpet, to be sure!

sp.speaker: Cockney.
sp.p: Vell done, old double drum!

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.p: Bravo! hurra! hurra!

sp.speaker: A Mec.
sp.p: I say, Jaques, how much did that ere coach cost?

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: I'm sure I can't say.

sp.speaker: Mec.
sp.p: Why, you ought to know—you paid for it.

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: So I did; that's a very just observation of yours. Look at those red flags! see how they're all laughing in the coaches! What a dinner we shall have! I'm always invited.

sp.speaker: Mec.
sp.p: They're laughing at you.

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: At me! what for?

sp.speaker: Cockney.
sp.p: Ah! vot for—tell us that, mister, since you're so werry vise?

sp.speaker: Mec.
sp.p: Because they're riding, and old Jaques is a-foot.

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: That's very true, too; and what's more, it ought not to be. I'll kick up a row, and next Lord Mayor's-day I'll have a coach all to myself, among them. They don't behave either honestly or respectfully to me—almost as bad as the government. Hillo! there's a hand in my pocket! my handkerchief's gone!

sp.speaker: Cockney.
sp.p: This is the man wot prigged it!

sp.speaker: Old Thief.
sp.p: No sich thing.

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: You did; it must have been you.
You've passed it away among your pals; but I know you stole it!

sp.speaker: Old Thief.
sp.p: Prove your words, mister?

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: Why, I had a fine handsome handkerchief in my left-hand coat pocket, and now it's gone. I had it a minute ago, and you've been standing close behind me longer than that!

sp.speaker: Old Thief.
sp.p: Ah! you're superficial.

sp.speaker: Voices.
sp.p: Ha! ha! ha! a regular old prig's evasion; an hereditary answer.

sp.speaker: A Constable.
sp.p: Make way, fellows, make way.

sp.speaker: A Dustman.
sp.p: Who do you call fellows?

sp.speaker: 2nd. Dustm.
sp.p: Does you mean to say we're fellows?

sp.speaker: Cockney.
sp.p: Knock off his gallus cocked-hat!

sp.speaker: A Policeman.
sp.p: Come, stand back here, stand back!

div.stage: [They fall back. Exit procession. Crowd follow in a stream. Two Mechanics remain.

sp.speaker: 1st. Mec.
sp.p: Well, so much for that; and what's the good of it?

sp.speaker: 2nd. Mec.
sp.p: Ah, but where's the harm of it? The Lord Peter's a good man.

sp.speaker: 1st. Mec.
sp.p: No doubt of it; but I'm tired of shows.

sp.speaker: Dust.
sp.p: The devil take the foremost, I say; aye, and for the matter o' that, all that follow.

sp.speaker: 2nd. Mec.
sp.p: Don't you say a word agin the Lord Mayor.

sp.speaker: Dust.
sp.p: Who's a-speaking agin him? Lawnic's the best one we've had this many a year; only I hates all this here expense and swanderation; not that I grudges him being Lord Mayor,
sp.stage: (shaking the ashes out of his pipe, and folding his arms,)

sp.speaker: 1st. Mec.
sp.p: Fat Jaques had much better spend his money in helping twenty thousand mechanics and other producers to a day's meal, than in overgorging a few hundred aldermen, and placemen, and fat knaves of all sorts.

sp.speaker: 2nd. Mec.
sp.p: See there!—there go a lot of 'em to dinner, with their stomach-pumps under their arms!

div.stage: Enter Fat Jaques, stamping with rage.

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: O, monstrous and unparalleled injustice! O, shame of my years and grey hairs!

sp.speaker: 2nd. Mec.
sp.p: What's the matter, Jaques?

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: Here's a pretty infamous pass things are come to!

sp.speaker: 1st. Mec.
sp.p: What fresh calamity has happened?

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: The last and worst! oh, shameful act!

sp.speaker: Dust.
sp.p: Out vith it—let's have it.

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: I'm not invited to the dinner!!

sp.speaker: 2nd. Mec.
sp.p: Not invited! well, never mind.

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: Oh, I won't be pacified; don't attempt to pacify me.

sp.speaker: 2nd. Mec.
sp.p: It's too bad, though.

sp.speaker: 1st. Mec.
sp.p: And you have paid for so many dinners!

sp.speaker: Dustman.
sp.p: Ha! ha! ha! sarve you right, old boy.

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: And this is not the worst of it either. I'll set fire to the city!

sp.speaker: 1st. Mec.
sp.p: No, don't.

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: I will—I'll fire the city, and roast every alderman in it—and then who's for crackling?

sp.speaker: Dust.
sp.p: And pray vot is the vurst of it? Did the Lord Mayor meet you in person at the hall door, and spit in your eye?

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: Oh no, not he, bless his heart! but there was a regular sealed official order sent down from the Quarter-deck house of nobles to say, that I was not to be admitted to the City dinner; no, nor on board any one of the barges; because they said I'd been obstropperous of late, and they feared I should make radical speeches over the bottle.

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.p: Shame! shame!

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: But I won't put up with it; in fact I can't bear it any longer.

sp.speaker: Dust.
sp.p: Here's a pretty kettle o' fish!

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: Where?—Oh, you're mocking me! Bear it I will not; I've said the word, and I'll keep it.

sp.speaker: Dust.
sp.p: Suppose you make a speech here?

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: Well, so I will.

div.stage: Enter Cockney, with a crowd of Mechanics, Manufacturers, poor Shop-keepers and others.

sp.speaker: Dust.
sp.p: Silence, gentlemen, silence! Mr. Jaques—called Fat, and looking so; but still werry empty—is going to make us a speech.

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.p: Hurra! let's hear! silence!

div.stage: [Fat Jaques gets upon the highest step of a door.

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: Gentlemen, I wish to know if a man who works hard from sun-rise to sun-set, and has done this all his life, is not to be considered a valuable member of any community of mankind, and as such to be respected?

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.p: Hear! hear! to be sure!

sp.speaker: Dust.
sp.p: Silence!

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: I wish to know if such a man consents to give the earnings of his labour towards the support of superior ranks in society, whether he ought not, in common generosity, to be allowed to retain enough for his own necessities, and even his comforts?

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.p: Of course; hear! hear!

sp.speaker: Dust.
sp.p: Silence, I say!

sp.speaker: Cockney.
sp.p: Silence!

sp.speaker: Dust.
sp.p: Hold your tongue, you young varmint!

sp.speaker: Cockney.
sp.p: Vy, a'nt I as much right to speak as you?

sp.speaker: Dust.
sp.p: If you doesn't hold your d---d sarcy tongue, I'll beat you into the vurst of cat's-meat with this here bell!

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.p: Silence!

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: Not to mention generosity, whether he ought not to be allowed that portion for which he stipulates,—in common justice, in common decency; nay more, in common honesty?

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.p: Bravo! bravo! hear! hear!

sp.speaker: Dust.
sp.p: Silence, the lower orders!

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: This small portion for our necessities and comforts, our lords and masters, and spiritual pastors' do not allow us: therefore, they have no common generosity; no justice; no decency; and not common ∗∗∗!

sp.speaker: Cockney.
sp.p: Bra-voo!

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.p: Bravo! bravo! huzza! bravo!

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: Finally; if they persist in not allowing us to keep that small portion which is our right, then we will peaceably take what we consider to be our share; and in future work only for ourselves.

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.p: Huzza! bravo! down with all hereditary rogues! bravo!

div.stage: Enter a posse of Police Soldiers.

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.p: Here's the police! look out! here they come!

sp.speaker: Inspector.
sp.p: Charge the rioters.

div.stage: [Police rush upon the crowd, who all run away. Fat Jaques is seized.

sp.p: Rescue! rescue!

div.stage: [Fat Jaques is taken to the Station-house without opposition.

div.head: SCENE III.
div.stage: A PRIVATE ORATORY IN THE PALACE OF THE RIGHT REV. FATHER IN GOD, BABEL, BY DIVINE RIGHT, BISHOP OF BABYLON.
Enter Bishop Babel and Earl Trampleneck.

lg.l: Not so, my friend; thy generous ardour sweeps,
Like to a fiery javelin o'er the targe,
Gaining applause by singeing distant fields,
But errant of the aim. The best of zeal
Is dangerous if to itself resigned.
Be zealous, yet with policy; be firm
And bold of passion, but thy balance keep.
Be subtle as the lynx, and use its eyes;
But let the movements of the fermenting soul
Be not o'er charged or hasty, lest the cause
Crack and dismember, and the million seize,
And scatter to the winds, if once disjointed,
What else had stood a rock for coming ages,
As it hath stood in ages past.
No more!
Right Reverend Father, subtle art thou of speech,
And in the workings of thy countenance,
A meaning is imprinted of thy thoughts
And secret sensations, that conveys
More than all words. I would assume
Thy downy presence and demean so meek,
Thine equanimity of balanced power,
But that the labouring torrents of my soul
Struggle too hard for vent: can Reason's hand
Ape the sea deities, and bind them in?
Can it put down a subterranean fire,
As with a rod miraculous?—No, father:
And mark thou this—as well may vassal men
Strive to oppose, or with recoil fling back,
Up to the summit of the thundering rock,
The cataract—as my descending course.
Beware that thou descend not to the grave!
The Tempestornians are mere slaves, 'tis true;
But 'tis their ignorance—their prejudices,
Their blindness, and our cunning, keep them so;
Else were they giants, whom we could not curb;
Their thraldrom is their folly—they're not weak.
The better that—I love to cope with strength.
Give me the forest lion in his youth,
To grapple with; the uplifted elements,
Smiting the earth and sea; these are fit peers
For contest, where defeat brings no disgrace;
But when the vassal dares to beard his lord,
E'en victory soils the foot that treads him down.
Be calm, fierce soul,—intemperate truth thou speak'st:
Reserve thine energies for the fit hour,
And then thrust home!
Doubt not but I will do so.
Yet, were it well their rude attack to wait,
Rather than crush rebellion's cradled form?
For, sooner or later, come rebellion must.
True, it must come; but let us not appear
The aggressors—so that mother church may bear
No stain apparent, nor good colour want
For direst retribution on their heads.
Touch not the fruit till ripe; then swallow all!
Well hast thou said; and I must quell my pulse
With heavy reason, and cold judgment's lore,
Though 'tis like tomb-stones o'er an earthquake's birth.
Meantime, I will go smoulder midst the walls
Of my chateau, and strive to lie perdue,
In best accordance with the counsel sage
Of one who first grim slaughter's chains shall loose,
And loud proclaim the red birth of the sword!
Farewell, thou glorious peer of Tempestorn!
Farewell, bright arm of valour!
Folly go with thee
Yet they're of excellent use—these hot-brained men;
For, being managed in their boiling moods
While wisdom sees the policy of peace,
And at the fitting season well put in;
Like a sheath'd blade that slumbers through dark years,
And at the sudden trumpet's piercing call,
Flies i' the sun's face; so to good account

sp.speaker: 1st. Shop.
sp.p: What in the world am I to do? I can't pay these taxes if it were to save my life—I owe two quarters, and haven't anything like the money!

sp.speaker: 2nd. Shop.
sp.p: You must do as others do—let them seize.

sp.speaker: 1st. Shop.
sp.p: By which I shall lose two hundred per cent. Think of my labour employed, and that of my workmen, in making those cabinets and rose-wood tables,—a pretty thing to put these up to auction for any thing they'll fetch!

sp.speaker: 2nd. Shop.
sp.p: Ah! they fall eventually into the hands of some lord or bishop, who gets them for a song.

lg.l: It makes my blood boil.
We turn what else would ruin any cause,
Startling our ambush'd plots into the light,
Like a foil'd tiger to be hunted down.
No, no,—we'll manage better. Trampleneck
Is ours, and that's enough. Lord Normanrust,
With all his old retainers, the vast wealth
And sweeping interest of Creamlandshire,
With other nobles, are our sure allies;
Since their own fortunes rise or fall with ours.
Queen Sinister's a cool, keen-sighted dame;
She much affecteth Bagnetlodge—'tis well.
Their plan is deep-laid, yet Earl Oldenvice
Hangs back reluctant,—craving, and fearing all things!
We'll do without his aid. Duke Bloodmansdorf,
Or Bagnetlodge, may to ∗∗∗∗ ascend.
I'll give my ear to both; but still incline
In actual purpose to the ---n's approved.
So shall the Church its tottering fabric rear
To heaven once more upon its former rock;
High spiring in its old authority,
The herd of men shall gild it with their toil,
And let the stars wink at us as they may.

sp.speaker: 2nd. Shop.
sp.p: And even if a lord gave a fair price for your whole stock,—after long credit, and your not daring to ask for your money,—the sum would not equal that which you pay every year above him in unfair taxation. There's no justice in the ∗∗∗∗ of Tempestorn,—it is all a sheer system of robbing tradesmen and poor people.

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: O the particular set of brutes, these Babylonish magistrates:—the lowest pit of perdition is too good for them!

sp.speaker: 2nd. Shop.
sp.p: Why, they seem to have let you off your recent affair pretty quickly—you've no reason to grumble.

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: Nor any reason to feel for other people—that's what you mean. But I do, and I grumble as much for them as myself.

sp.speaker: 1st. Shop.
sp.p: Why for yourself?

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: First, because I was dragged to the station-house for making a patriotic speech; secondly, that although I made no resistance to the regular police authority myself, nor did any one lift a hand for my rescue (loud as they bawled instead), I was nevertheless beaten over the shoulders and crown of my head by their brutal truncheons—see, here's a bump, and I'm all over black and blue and yellow bruises besides, and was half strangled, into the bargain, as we say in trade: thirdly, I was badgered by the inspector at the station-house; my story not fairly heard—the policemen are always believed before any gentleman—and my person contaminated by the vermin that swarmed in the dark room where they locked me up in company with a most depraved drunken crowd of various sexes. What a dreadful scene it would have been for my wife—and me too—had she come there after me! Fourthly, I was kept there all night. Fifthly, I was taken before the magistrates in the morning, and snubbed and bullied by them before I was suffered to say a word in my own defence. Sixthly, the policemen told barefaced lies; contradicted everything I said; then contradicted themselves; then brazened it out, and were complimented by the magistrates for doing their duty.

sp.speaker: 1st. Shop.
sp.p: But how came you to get off so soon?—By bail, to a large amount, perhaps?

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: To be sure, and my own recognizances to five times as much more. They know I shall be getting again into some scrape or other, before long—a dead robbery, you see.

sp.speaker: 2nd. Shop.
sp.p: But you said you grumbled as much on account of others as yourself: all this is about yourself only.

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: Ah, Mr. Higgins! what I could tell you about the brutish conduct of the Babylonish magistrates towards poor people, would fill a volume—that ought to fill your eyes with tears, and the whole city with groans, as it does my heart with disgust, hatred, and execration. There, in a big-wigged court of injustice, I saw a poor girl committed to prison for trying to sell some nick-nacks of her own making, in order to support her mother and four children besides herself: there, I saw a destitute woman, the wife of a soldier, to whom she was journeying, committed to prison, with her three hungry children, for being found “huddled together,” as she said, in the cold streets at night, having no bed to go to, or money to procure food; there, I saw thieving encouraged by the remorseless persecution of honest poverty;— there, I saw some hungry-looking boys ordered a sound flogging, partly for the trivial offence of stealing a pen'orth of apples, but chiefly to patronise some Jack in office—at the Old Belly, of course, because the fees for a flogging are treble there to what they are at Clerkman's-knell;—there I saw palpable nakedness and ghostly famine mocked at, and called mere cant, and sent to prison—except the miserable wretch besought the magistrate with agonised earnestness to be sent there, to escape starvation, and then the object was compelled to depart. No, Mr. Higgins; you mistake the true Tempestornian character if you think I do not feel these things deeply. The habitual conduct of the Babylonian magistrates towards the destitute, is enough to make the poor tear up the pavements, and dash the ∗∗∗∗ out as they go home to dinner. I wonder some famishing man does not sacrifice his worthless life in making a grill of one of these heartless storks— they're not men!

sp.speaker: 2nd. Shop.
sp.p: Why don't you do it yourself?

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: I've got a shop to look after as well as you.

sp.speaker: 2nd. Shop.
sp.p: And there, I fear, begins, centres, and ends, all our patriotism.

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: No, but I've got a great many shops.

sp.speaker: 2nd. Shop.
sp.p: The same argument holds.

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: Well, but you see, Mr. Higgins, I'm not placed in a similar position, just yet. I've a great many farms and manufactories, and merchandise, and all sorts of things; and although my affairs are deeply and thoroughly involved, still I can't be said to be in want of a dinner.

sp.speaker: 2nd. Shop.
sp.p: Exactly: you wait till that happens, and then it will be too late.

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: No, it wont' though.

sp.speaker: 1st. Shop.
sp.p: It would be too late to do any good to the country—that is, the shop-keepers. See what a situation I'm in? I expect my goods to be seized every hour for those cursed assessed taxes. What would you advise me to do, Mr. Jaques?

sp.speaker: 2nd. Shop.
sp.p: Stand still.

sp.speaker: 1st. Shop.
sp.p: I did'nt speak to you:
would you advise me to stand still?

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: What, and let them rob you of your property?—it's hardly in flesh and blood to bear that, whatever else one bears.

sp.speaker: 2nd. Shop.
sp.p: Why, you've borne it all your life!

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: Yes, but they now do it openly, and without the least ceremony or decorum—they tell us they will have the taxes! This makes all the difference.

sp.speaker: 1st. Shop.
sp.p: Not all, for we're not able to pay now.

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: True, I had forgot that. Well then, I think we really can't do better than stand still—that is, as still as we can.

sp.speaker: 1st. Shop.
sp.p: But the people won't suffer it— perhaps the mob will interfere and beat off the officers—we can't help that, you know?

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: No, to be sure not—ha! ha! God forbid we should.

sp.speaker: 2nd. Shop.
sp.p: I'm no better situated myself, than the rest: if my goods are not seized this time, they will next—it's impossible to meet such extortionary demands. Look at all these large houses— these mansions of the great! Unequal taxation enables them to stand, in spite of their gambling, their luxury, and ocean-like extravagance; while honest tradesmen are ruined in spite of their economy and industry early and late. I'm sick of my life, and begin not to care a d---n for anything.

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: I begin to come to my senses.

sp.speaker: 1st. Shop.
sp.p: What is the use of all our honest endeavours? See the pains we take to go to the cheapest market, get the cheapest workmen, tell the most plausible lies to our customers—for apt lies are the essence of a good salesman—and yet we can scarcely live; for just as we have covered our expenses and begin to make profit, come the accursed taxes that sweep away all the produce of our toil. I wish to my soul the mob would do something, for we might almost as well shut up shop as keep it open!

sp.speaker: 2nd. Shop.
sp.p: And you would applaud from the house top?

sp.speaker: 1st. Shop.
sp.p: That I would—or rather within the house, for we need not show ourselves: our hearts, you know, may be with them just the same.

sp.speaker: 2nd. Shop.
sp.p: Provided they do our property no mischief, you mean?

sp.speaker: 1st. Shop.
sp.p: Yes, of course—we suffer enough from government.

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: Well, come this way—let's have some bread and cheese, and porter, and hope for better times.

sp.speaker: 2nd. Shop.
sp.p: Better times won't come of themselves.

div.head: SCENE V.
div.stage: Enter a Beggar in tatters, with a wooden leg.

sp.speaker: Beg.
sp.p: Tol-de-rol de rol day! Begging's a very different thing now to what it wor seven years agone. I've sarved an apprenticeship to it, and by this time I knows my business as well as e'er a beggar on town; but I can hardly make out a living now. There's no money in the country, that's for sartin. Howsomedever, tol-de-rol de ri day!

div.stage: Enter Two other Beggars, with threadbare coats and ragged aprons.

sp.speaker: Beg.
sp.p: Oho! here's opposition in the field; I'll stump myself off.

sp.speaker: 2nd. Beg.
sp.p: Stop a bit, old boy; we shan't ruin you by the Competitive system—there's no one near to try our luck upon.

sp.speaker: 1st. Beg.
sp.p: There's windows to the houses, and a copper might fall as from heaven; though there's more likelihood of wind and rain, and charity slops; nevertheless, there's some chance of browns, so I'll hop off to another place.

sp.speaker: 2nd. Beg.
sp.p: Ah, you've plied all up the street, and we've no hope.

sp.speaker: 1st. Beg.
sp.p: I b'lieve you're right there; and moreover than that, you looks werry like raw recruits.

sp.speaker: 3rd. Beg.
sp.p: Yes, indeed, we are; we're not used to this sort of business at all.

sp.speaker: 2nd. Beg.
sp.p: We're mechanics, and very ready to work, but can't get any, so we're driven to this for means of existence.

sp.speaker: 3rd. Beg.
sp.p: Or for the chance of it, rather. We have not had anything given us all day, and we're almost famished. But you were singing when we turned the corner?

sp.speaker: 1st. Beg.
sp.p: Vy you see as I sleeps in the street— obleeged to it of late, times are so hard—in course I gets up werry early. I've been at it since five this morning, and only got a single brown; but just now I picked up one out of the gutter, so that finds me a roll and half a pint o'beer. Who's a better cause to sing than the man who in these here flinty times has got a dinner in his belly, or his pocket?

sp.speaker: 3rd. Beg.
sp.p: Very true, very true; I wish we had a right to sing.

sp.speaker: 2nd. Beg.
sp.p: How did you lose your leg?

sp.speaker: 1st. Beg.
sp.p: Nine years ago I was under-groom to Lord Oldenvice; and once as he was out riding on a horse what was his betters, the horse having 'nation objection to spurs, found his sides werry coolly let blood in profoosion, so he flung my Lord on the road and bolted. His foot stuck in the stirrup, and I was just off my horse in time—for I seed what was going to happen—to seize the reins and save his precious life, ven the horse in rewenge tipt me a hint of his natur, and broke my leg all to splinters.

sp.speaker: 3rd. Beg.
sp.p: Well, but didn't he give you a pension? I've always heard he was famous at giving pensions to retire?

sp.speaker: 1st. Beg.
sp.p: He ordered my discharge as soon as I could go on crutches. He said, what use was a groom with one leg!—and he couldn't afford, in justice to his family, to pay wages for nothing, and keep idlers about his house. Three months after, when I was werry poor and distressed, I sent him in a petition that he would pay the bill for this here wooden pin; but he said as how he knew nothing whatsomedever about sich things. So after working as well as I could, here and there, and trying in vain to get into the verkus, and then sweeping roads and what not, I was obligated to take to begging, and here I is!

div.stage: Enter a Gentleman of the Court. First Beggar hobbles up to him.

sp.speaker: 1st. Beg.
sp.p: Lord bless your honour! I hopes your Lordship will bestow a trifle upon a poor fellow that hasn't had a single bit of bread to eat these three days? So help me, your honour, as true as I stands here, I haven't a single halfpenny in the world, and all the blessed Saints in the cullender know I speaks truth!

sp.speaker: Courtier.
sp.p: Get away with you!

sp.speaker: 1st. Beg.
sp.p: I lost my leg, your honour, at the Battle of Trafalgar; and I've sailed all the world over with his Majesty Lord Nelson; and there isn't a battle what you've heard tell on, that I've not been in. I hopes your honour—

sp.speaker: 2nd. Beg.
sp.p: Pray sir, consider our condition.

sp.speaker: Cour.
sp.p: Get out of my way, you scoundrels!

sp.speaker: 3rd. Beg.
sp.p: Pray sir,—

sp.speaker: 1st. Beg.
sp.p: What business have you to interfere with my man? He was mine first—you must larn better manners!

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.p: I'll teach you all better manners. Come along with me—if you offer the least resistance, I'll split your skulls with my truncheon, before you can cry Jack Robinson.

sp.speaker: 1st. Beg.
sp.p: Now, then, mister! Vot harm have we done, I should like to know?

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.p: Come along with you all three! Their Worships have come to a determination to punish all destitute vagrants with the utmost rigour; and 'specially all beggars.—I heard you all begging of that ere gentleman.

sp.speaker: 1st. Beg.
sp.p: No sich thing, mister.

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.p: I saw you all in the act, and that's as good. You will get three months at the tread-mill, every man jack of you,—come along!

sp.speaker: 1st. Beg.
sp.p: Oh! that I'd snatched his gold seals with his ticker at the end of 'em, and made off while t'others bothered him for browns!

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.p: Come along with you.

sp.speaker: 2nd. Beg.
sp.p: Petty larceny is safer than begging —we shan't forget this lesson when we get out of prison!

sp.speaker: 3rd. Beg.
sp.p: My poor hungry wife—my poor dying children!

sp.speaker: Pol.
sp.p: Come along, I say, you beggarly rascals.

div.head: SCENE VI.
div.stage: Enter Three Noblemen-Footmen, in rich liveries.

lg.l: What says thou, gallant nabob, to that pun?
It's well enough, but too canaille.
That's true.
Sir Bob forgets himself at times, although
He's of so high a family;—methinks
This knee-buckle shines well?
On such a calf,
How should it otherwise?
Ha! ha! ha!
It seems as if you meant that trash for wit.
I meant it, gentlemen, for what it is.
Were you at the Italian Opera last night?
You were not at the club.
Our people went,
But I was otherwise engaged at home.
What a fine singer is that Malibran!
A splendid creature too—I'd marry her.
Humph! not so splendid neither: she's too thin.
Ah, but I like her spirit; hang your fat!—
una voce poco fat.
Pray cease your noise, why do you play such pranks?
What's that to you, sir knight of woful phiz?
While the sun shines I'll gambol in his rays;
Were they not made for jolly boys like us?
We eat, we drink o'the best the world affords;
No care have we for how the gold's obtain'd;
And sleep in beds of down. Let fools drudge on,
Sweating and grinding—groaning at the plough,
Groping in mines, or starving at the loom;
Our dial's hand points but to one bright hour,
For all its circle brings the self-same joy.
Well done, I swear.
Why yes, that's well indeed.
Think you this aiguillette hangs gracefully?
There's such a turbot at our house to-day;
And only three o' the family at home!
P'rhaps you'll drop in?

sp.speaker: 3rd. Foot.
sp.p: What wine d'ye have?

sp.speaker: 2nd. Footman.
sp.p: Come, let's be off: what dirty fellow's this?

sp.speaker: Mec.
sp.p: You'd look dirty too, sir, if you had no soap found you. Those who are wretchedly hungry and have no means of getting a meal, can't spare time to care or think of how they look. I hope, sir, you'll see if you can't find me a small trifle?

sp.speaker: 1st. Foot.
sp.p: I say, my lord, here's “poco fat” again!

sp.speaker: 3rd. Foot.
sp.p: Get away, fellow,—come, I sha'nt stay here.

sp.speaker: 2nd. Foot.
sp.p: Let's see, my man?

sp.speaker: Mec.
sp.p: Oh pray do, sir! I'm in real distress, I assure you.

sp.speaker: 2nd. Foot.
sp.p: What is your trade, my man?

sp.speaker: Mec.
sp.p: A journeyman carpenter, sir; but I haven't been able to get a bit o'work these three weeks.

sp.speaker: 3rd. Foot.
sp.p: That's very strange, there's so many new buildings continnerly being herected!

sp.speaker: Mec.
sp.p: And I've a wife, too, just laying-in.

sp.speaker: 3rd. Foot.
sp.p: Come, what do you stay here for?

sp.speaker: 2nd. Foot.
sp.p: Ah! well my man, I've got nothing for you.

sp.speaker: 1st. Foot.
sp.p: See, here's a motley group of the populace coming this way!

sp.speaker: 2nd. Foot.
sp.p: Quick, or we shall be covered with vermin.

div.stage: Enter some Patlanders, Bricklayers, Masons, and a Crowd of starving People, all clamorously following Fat Jaques.

sp.speaker: 1st. Brick.
sp.p: Be jazes! and we're the boys that will niver lave ye at all, misther Jaques; so we won't.

sp.speaker: 2nd. Brick.
sp.p: Not so long as we've a single dacent-covered leg to go upon—nor after!

sp.speaker: A Mason.
sp.p: Niver lave you, misther Jaques, till you put us in the way of arning a male now!

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: I can't do more than is possible!

sp.speaker: 1st. Brick.
sp.p: Och! and my sowl upon you, but you must do more than that, for die in the dirty strates we can't wid any comfort or propriety at all, my ould jewel!

sp.speaker: Omnes.
sp.p: Why are we to die in the streets? What is to become of us?

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: What can I do,—what would you have me do?

sp.speaker: A Mason.
sp.p: Och! and lave off building huge places for the government, and give us some of the money instead, just by way of raising our past wages, which were only three-pence a day. Och! heart alive o' me now, what's the good of all these fine buildings to the poor people who build them! Little's the pay we get to kape enough strength in our bodies to work with; and when all's complate and dacent, the noblemen-folk and tun-bellied praists, get fat in them, by raison o' the taxes set on the edifices.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: Yes, the Priests and the Nobles get fat on the Taxes!—They grind our bones to make them bread.

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: You confuse my brain— you turn my head!

sp.speaker: Mason.
sp.p: And a good job too, honey; for it's been turned so long that a fresh twist might set it in the right place again. Ought not those who build the big places, I say to you again—ought not the workmen to have a small share of the taxes, instead of those who do nothing for anybody but themselves? Och! if the paple were all of my mind, we'd soon have a traty with France or America, and pawn St. Paul's, and half the lords' palaces, so we would!

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: I wish we could,—I wish we could —I'm very sorry we built them at all; the more we do, the more we may; besides being treated all the worse for what we have done.

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: Bravo! bravo! now you speak like a man.

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: Yes, yes, and I mean to act up to it; and so do you all, my fellow-citizens, and countrymen,—Tempestornians, Pat-landers, Plaidsmen, and all others whose liberal feelings are matter of fact. Nor is this the first time I have spoke out my mind. I have done so to their faces —upon my soul, I have—upon several occasions recently. I was driven to it. Have I not complained and groaned for years?—have I not again and again represented to the haughty Nobles, the dreadful state we were in? Have I not declared to them, that the people were driven half mad by continued oppression, and would not bear the injustice any longer? But to what purpose? Though I have exhorted these pampered Lords in coronets and mitres, with thousands of starving People in my train, echoing my words,—artisans, mechanics manufacturers, labourers, and an army of poor martyr-faced curates, praying of them to think of those who did all God's work in the church— haven't these conservative cormorants stood with a supercilious deaf ear to my entreaties, swearing allegiance over the crown, in order to help themselves with the gold that over-flowed even the vast measure of its preposterous ∗∗∗?

sp.speaker: A Brick.
sp.p: And, by the mass, your big rogues, the Tempestornian nobles, have cut us off from their feelings, as nate as a whistle! and now we'll sarve them the same in matter-o'-fact,—tunder and turf!—down wid the Union to the bottom o' the emerald sea!

sp.speaker: Voices.
sp.p: The divell fly fast away wid your lying Union!

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: It will grieve my soul to lose you, but what's to be done?—I can't blame you. You're treated most infamously; but you see how they treat me!

sp.speaker: Voices.
sp.p: We do! we do!—if you choose to bear it, be jazes we won't!

sp.speaker: 1st Brick.
sp.p: Och! and blythe was the day my mother sent me clane and nate out o' the cabin in a gentayle new suit, wid the time o' day in my pocket—and it's dirty I shall go back. Besides that same ticker in my fob, I had money and rings, and a sartin-sure five acres of grayne faylds, all in lovely flower, so soon as I raiched the age of manhood; and plenty of—

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: Come, come; I can't believe all this you know.

sp.speaker: 1st Brick.
sp.p: Och! 'twas true for me.

sp.speaker: Manufac.
sp.p: What's to become of us and our families!—we can get no work, and no food?

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: No food at all!—but I begin to find there are many thousands in the same situation. By the lord, I'm not without fears that I shall soon be in the same plight myself, with all that belong to me!

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: You will! you will!

sp.speaker: Cock.
sp.p: I'll bet you a tanner he won't though? —what is it?

sp.speaker: A Brick.
sp.p: Fait, mister Jaques, times have exparienced the divell's own alteration wid you Once,—it's a long while ago,—you could plaise your dillicate pallate wid all the swate illigancies o' the saison and out of saison; you indulged in your poetical fancies for delightful rarities, fraquently ordering for your dinner a young jackass and sausages, or a chimney-sweeper stuffed with ten crows; but now, by my sowl!—

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: Very true,—very true,— Oh, you gormandizing fellow!—but you're brought to short commons now!

sp.speaker: Mason.
sp.p: This way, my lads o' the Emerald Isle; let's lave this old gintleman, who won't help himself or us from slavery, so long as he can get enough to ate and drink!

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: I see my errors; I see how wrong I have been—my eyes are opened now—I have come to my proper senses at last.

sp.speaker: Manufac. and Labourers.
sp.p: So have we!— but what shall we do for bread?—It's of no use to apply to the parish, or anywhere else,—we're called impostors, till we're stone dead.

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: Something shall and must be done!

sp.speaker: Cock.
sp.p: Something else must now be done!

div.stage: [They all range themselves round Fat Jaques, who acts as Leader of the Chorus.

lg.l: I do object to starve!
We, one and all declare upon our oaths—
And thus we miserable men on ragged knees,
Now plight our keen-felt troths—
That far from having meat to carve,
Or e'en a quarten loaf to halve,
Or share in slices;
Much less the dreamy luxury of smelling cheese;
We have not had a wholesome meal this month!
But we protest
That our distress and wild unrest,
Though preached at by fat heroes of the Tenth,
And our unnumbered woes
And wants, of food and clothes,
Are not so many vices!
I do object to feed the men who starve me,
Yet if I do not work, threaten to halve me!
I will be rather slaughter'd—
Hung, drawn, and quarter'd—
Than longer be the horse denied his corn,
His water, and his grass;
Yet whose bare ribs are lash'd to toil each morn,
With no more strength than in an empty basket,
To make vast wealth—bread, meat, and well-filled flasket—
For some hereditary ass!
This is the simple question:
Are we born slaves, or free?
In this immense white nation,
Worse than the blacks o'er sea?
If slaves—where is our portion
Of beast-of-burden food?
If free—give us the option
Of choosing masters good:
Give all the right of voting
For men who will uphold—
The justice of our having
The filings of our gold.
If labour is not gold, I swear
There is no other coin,
For all the crowns that sovereigns wear
Are Labour's “right divine.”

sp.speaker: Cockney.
sp.p: Here's the police coming!

sp.speaker: Voices.
sp.p: Where! let's be off—we shall be taken up as rioters.

sp.speaker: Fat. Jaq.
sp.p: It is the police, I declare, as I'm a sinner!—here they come! There's two or three soldiers among them! See, they're getting out their truncheons of office!

sp.speaker: A Manufac.
sp.p: What's their office to us? An't we Tempestornians born as well as they? Their office makes no difference!

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: Oh, but it does though!—here they come pell-mell at us—don't you see the King's arms? I dare say they've got written orders for all this in their pockets!

sp.speaker: Manufac.
sp.p: Down with them!

sp.speaker: Cockney.
sp.p: Let's get some flag-stones, and crack the raw lobsters!

div.stage: Enter a posse of Policemen. They rush towards the Crowd.

sp.speaker: Several Voices.
sp.p: Stand fast; down with them!

div.stage: [Police charge the crowd, who all take to their heels, in disorder. Many are knocked down with fractured skulls and broken arms.

div.head: SCENE I.
div.stage: A LARGE LAWN, EXTENDING ALONG ONE WING OF THE PALACE OF LORD NORMANRUST—TIME, NIGHT.
Enter Lord Normanrust, abstractedly. He is clad in complete armour.

sp.speaker: Lord Norm.

lg.l: Our years roll onward, cloud succeeding cloud,
Tempest and calm—gloom and celestial light:
Spring in her verdant robe, with dews besprent,
Glistening in virgin purity, ascends
From our luxuriant earth, smiling sweet peace
Over the votive meadow-fields and woods:
Then Summer lifts his regal head, and shakes
From aurean locks broad sun-shine o'er our towers;
Till Autumn with his honest visage comes,
Sturdy and harvest-bronzed, to bend the knee,
And downward turn his wreath'd horn's crimson mouth,
Out-pouring fruits resplendent at our feet.
Then patriarch Winter's old heraldic shape,
Bearded with snow, grotesque, and rocky limb'd;
Strikes with his ringing club the brittle earth;
Sends anarchy into the forest wild;
The mean hut desolates, the farm, the flocks
But howls excluded from the wassail hall!
Why should this good be marr'd? Why should men change,
By innovation's dangerous visiting,
These excellent arrangements of the world?
As well admit a dragon to your house,
And not expect it soon to change its master
Who that hath sense can sleep i'the fold of peace
When war prowls round, like to a hungry wolf?
I have been meditating if 'twere safe
Or rational to accede to man's desire—
And grant the people some few favours more
Than they possess at present;—but I know
They are insatiate—whate'er they gain,
More will be asked, till they throw off all shame,
Like an old mantle—for 'tis now well rent,
And thro' the gaps we see rebellion's flesh—
And boldly seek for freedom in everything.
It shall not—ought not—must not—cannot be!

sp.stage: [Pauses. Then lifts himself proudly, and continues.

lg.l: Our ancestors, with firm commanding power
United, urged the glorious car of day
With conduct safe to its alternate goals.
Let not a craven spirit then, infuse
Adulterate yieldings in our purposes,
That soon would prove us retrograde and weak,
Changing our Order to a common sign
For mobs to pelt at, feast there, or harangue;
(Inducing such equality i' the end,
That we may e'en be jostled in the street
With less excuse, apology, or awe,
Than if we were some alderman or mayor;)
Or else by choosing the intermediate course,
Half granting, half refusing popular claims—
Which only acts as fuel to resolve—
Lose in proportion our accustomed power;
And thus disjointed, when strong tempests rise,
Bring down our 'scutcheons' ancient blazonry
In shatters to the dust—where lay our heads!
Night, in her ebon mail, whose diamond studs
Rivet in myriads those colossal folds,
Recumbent on a heap of alpine clouds,
Now gazes o'er our earth. Ye rolling orbs,
That with unwasting urns of varied fire,
Burn onward round the eternal Dial—worlds,
Thronging perchance with life, yet to our ken
Pois'd as the bright theogony of heaven,
Circling the solar throne of Jove—how clear
To mortal minds the emblem do ye show
Of necessary magnitude and grades!
Nerve then your souls, ye Tempestornian peers,
And buckle on your bright ancestral mail!
Stride through the capitol's Babylonian roar,
In lofty scorn; and when the struggle comes,
Bethink ye of hereditary glories—
Of well-won banners, vassals, and domains—
Of God, our right, and of the stars above.

div.head: SCENE II.
div.stage: A NARROW COURT-YARD, AT THE BACK OF THE HOUSE OF THE EARL OF OLDENVICE.—TIME, AS BEFORE.
Enter the Earl of Oldenvice. (looks upward a long while at the stars.)

sp.speaker: Earl of Olden.
sp.p: I wish I had the money that all those are worth!

div.head: SCENE III.
div.stage: INTERIOR OF THE HOUSE OF FAT JAQUES. FAT JAQUES AND MRS. JAQUES DISCOVERED SEATED BY A LARGE FIRE-PLACE, WITH A FEW EMBERS IN IT.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Jaq.
sp.p: I will not hear of it, Jaques, not for a moment; these Political Unions, and Trades Unions, and Co-operative Meetings, are no good, depend on it. You're always getting yourself into some scrape or other; it 'ill end in your ruin, mark my words if it don't!

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: Well, but my dear! how can a man bear to be put upon as I have been all these years, and not resent it; and with no chance of their behaving better, either? Only think of the wretched state of bankruptcy to which all my sons, who are out in the world, have been reduced! I can't do any more for them, and yet you want me to be quiet!

sp.speaker: Mrs. Jaq.
sp.p: It does not signify talking, Jaques, go you shan't to any more of these meetings; they only unhinge your mind, and make you ill in body and temper, and fit for nothing. What you say about oppression and infamous treatment, and the remorseless covetousness of the nobles and clergy, may be all very true; but you know, Jaques, they're born our betters, and—

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: No, I'm d---d if they are!

sp.speaker: Mrs. Jaq.
sp.p: Well, but it's no use to talk in that mad way: you're not a lord, you know, nor a duke, nor a bishop, nor any thing like one!

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: Thank God!

sp.speaker: Mrs. Jaq.
sp.p: Now, do listen to reason, and mark my words if they don't come true. If you persist in these obstroppollous goings on, you'll be sent to prison, and stript of every individual thing you possess; after which—

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: They'll take my skin!—nothing else left!

sp.speaker: Mrs. Jaq.
sp.p: Now don't go on so, dear! No, they wouldn't flay you,—you'd be hung!

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: Humph! Much obliged to them for such a proof of their gratitude,—and to you, too, for the prophecy.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Jaq.
sp.p: It's all very well, Jaques, these Unions and Meetings, for those who have nothing to lose! But those who have—

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: Damme! I've nothing like what I once had!

sp.speaker: Mrs. Jaques.
sp.p: I know that. I know it as well as you, Jaques; all that you say is very true; I know it's all true; but then we have just enough to live upon, and maintain ourselves respectably; and do for God's sake, my dear, let us keep this as long as ever we can!

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: Well, well, dear, you're right; you're right; I'll try to follow your advice as close as possible: children all a-bed, I s'pose?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Jaq.
sp.p: Hours ago.

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: Who the devil's that?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Jaq.
sp.p: Oh! Bull-street officers, I dare-say, or the police, come to take you for something!

sp.speaker: Voice outside.
sp.p: Fat Jaques! Fat Jaques, I say! Why you're not gone to bed already, are you, old boy? Open the door.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Jaq.
sp.p: I know the voice; yes, I'm sure of it!

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: I an't, though!

sp.speaker: Voice outside.
sp.p: I see you both, standing like two fools in the middle of the room?

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: Ah! Yes, I know who it is; it's the Lord Jester of the Court; let him in.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Jaq.
sp.p: I wonder what he's come for at this time o' night?

div.stage: (They both run and open the door.)

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: Pray walk in, my lord.

div.stage: Enter the Right Silly the Dandy of Derrydown.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Jaq.
sp.p: Welcome, my lord! Would your lordship please to take a seat by the fire.

sp.speaker: Dan. of Derry.
sp.p: Thank ye, good woman—Ah! Mrs. Jaques, I presume?

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: Yes, my lord.

sp.speaker: Dan. of Derry.
sp.p: Ah! Pray don't let me put you out of your way at all. 'Tis a fine evening,—I've just left a rout, and discovered the air to be so clear and refreshing, that I alighted from my carriage, and actually walked unattended, except by one trusty valet, from the top of this street to your very door!

sp.speaker: Mrs. Jaq.
sp.p: A fine star-light night, please your lordship, an't it?

sp.speaker: Dan. of Derry.
sp.p: Ah, is it indeed? I never look up at such things; the gas-lamps are kept in excellent order!—In honour's fair truth, I haven't seen the moon this whole summer. In winter, of course, one has no chance. Ah! Jaques, my man, my good man, I have some private conversation for you. You've been much annoyed and vexed,— and, ah! they do say, taxed; and you've not been treated with the respect due to your industry and many excellent qualities,—ah!

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: I'm sure, I—I really feel deeply obliged by your kindness, my lord—really I—

sp.speaker: Mrs. Jaq.
sp.p: Yes, that we do, your lordship; poor Jaques has been very much troubled of late.

sp.speaker: Dan. of Derry.
sp.p: Well, never mind, good folks, there will soon be a stop put to these little et cæteras. His Grossness, the Duke of Bloodmansdorf, and his Expediency the Duke of Bagnetlodge, at the express desire of her Tartness the Queen, have sent me to look into your affairs.

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: Have—have—
have they indeed!

sp.speaker: Mrs. Jaq.
sp.p: Bless them all, say I; God save the King, and the Queen, and all the Royal Family!

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: I'm really deeply overcome by their condescension. What may be their commands to me?

sp.speaker: Dan. of Derry.
sp.p: In the first place, in consideration of your long and faithful services, it has been determined that you shall receive the order of Knighthood; to descend also, to the male heirs of your family, who shall hereafter be known by the title of Sir John-Bull Jaques.

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: Can this—can these noble tidings—can they be true?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Jaq.
sp.p: And I be my Lady John-Bull, too!

sp.speaker: Dan. of Derry.
sp.p: And your ladyship's eldest daughter, also.
But step aside with me a minute, Sir John-Bull, as I have another little matter to transact with you, by order of the Queen.

div.stage: (Jaques bows to the ground, and they go to a table at the opposite end of the room.)

sp.speaker: Mrs. Jaq.
sp.p: How right I have been all along in my advice to Jaques! I always told him to keep himself quiet, and not mix in politics, and attend radical meetings, and something would be done for him, some day or other. If he hadn't followed my advice, we should all have been shut up in a flea-breeding prison by this time, without a sixpence to help us out, or keep us comfortable in. Now, what a change has happened! He to be Sir Knight, and I My Lady, and our descendants to bear the same title in a generalogical stream down the long posteriority of our future line! I dreamt the other night of walking in a garden full of the tallest hollyhocks, all in flower; and I was just picking one to place in my bough-pot, when I awoke, and found myself pulling off Jaques's red night-cap by its tassel; and says I directly, this dream argues—what in the world is Jaques signing at that table?
What papers can those be that his lordship has just put in his pocket? The dockyments for our title, I suppose; and yet—

sp.speaker: Dan. of Derry.
sp.p: Good evening to you, Mrs. Jaques; pleasant dreams to your Ladyship—fal lal de ra!

div.stage: [Exit singing, and shaking Jaques by the hand indifferently.

lg.l: Now we shall see on the next Lord Mayor's day,
Whether I dine or no! Now, there's no doubt
But they will send an invitation,
Full of sweet words, as plums in their best pudding,—
The rich one, black with brandy, next the Mayor.
But 'tis not certain now, unless much pressed,
That Sir John Jaques will go!
What papers were those you signed?

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: Some of the patents for my title; the rest I had not time to read; besides I could not, they were so cramply written.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Jaq.
sp.p: But you didn't sign them?

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: Yes, I did; his lordship said it was necessary that the court should know if I still had enough property to support the title; and I imagine those papers were the estimate, which they knew well enough where to find; as I saw the words ‘manufactories, farms, coal-mines, shops, ships, merchandise, three per cent. consols,’ and such like, sprinkled about. And so I put my name.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Jaq.
sp.p: They must have been sprinkled very thick for you to have seen so many in so short a time, in a hand writing you could hardly make out!

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: That's true—what are you thinking at?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Jaq.
sp.p: His lordship called me Mrs. Jaques as he went out!

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: Yes, and your Ladyship too!

sp.speaker: Mrs. Jaq.
sp.p: And then he sang fal de riddle!

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: Well, wha— what o' that, you fool?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Jaq.
sp.p: And you signed your real name to all those papers?

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: Yes, to be sure,—I believe so—F. Jaques,—he told me!

sp.speaker: Mrs. Jaq.
sp.p: Yes!—

sp.speaker: Fat Jaq.
sp.p: Ye—yes, he did!

div.stage: [They stand opposite each other, pale and confounded. Scene closes.

lg.l: 'Tis true a crown's a toy; but high ambition
Is like a child, until that toy's obtain'd.
Events now float it tow'rds me: one more reach,
And I could ∗∗∗∗, methinks;
Yet should a sudden heave o' the mass of things,
Bear it a span beyond, I then should lose
My balance, and fall headlong in the deep.
Caution's a fool sometimes; the ∗∗∗ is mine
To all intents and purposes—the hour
Is near at hand, and shan't be miss'd.
Good morrow,
Most noble duke! I came to seek you here.
Aught fresh, beside the morn?
Yes, and worth knowing.
King Anchorbroke, with whom I supped last night,
Being well plied by me with foaming cups,
And lost to reason as the morn drew on,
Between strong hiccoughs, jests and sea-songs coarse,
And ludicrous efforts at collectedness,
Blurted all secrets out.
He has not many
Intrusted to his care; and of these few,
The most important are to me conveyed—
Sink in my thoughts, then buz within his ear.
Say, are they worthy mention?
I think they are,
And of your prompt arrangements. With fresh dogs
The king being hunted, worried, and confused,
Not anxious for Reform, yet fearing tumult
And popular convulsion, seems resolved
Huge taxes to repeal, and mulct the church;
Whereby the people, with a loud acclaim,
Will host him to fresh favour!
Humph! proceed.
Then will the people, never satisfied,
From step to step advance, thrusting the king
Like to the covering of a sacred shield,
Made from a sign-board, in their crowded van,
Accumulating thus propulsion strong
On his own primal movement; so that he
Cannot in common honesty recoil.
Good: but what evil do you thence foresee?
The worst. All taxes of the working classes
Will gradually be reduced; their strength
Of mind and body, with abundant food
Will fearfully increase; the spirit of change,
And love of liberty, are now abroad,
Which, if not stopped, will, like a sweeping flood
Poured over vineyards, gardens, parks, and meads,
Reduce all property to a level surface.
Equal taxation saps the nobles' power:
We cannot stand unless on 'vantage ground.
Aye, aye, all this is clear; but I deny
The evil you predict: 'tis not an evil
Until it come to pass;—we'll see to that.
Let the king sweep off taxes; 'tis no more
Than I myself would do, if premier;
Placing them elsewhere—on the people still—
Let the Wigs crow and victual, victual and crow;
One thing is certain—we must make a stand
Against all real innovation—
Against all actual freedom—thus to ∗∗
The People to ∗∗∗∗; then the king,
Driven on before them like a schoolboy's hoop,
Must crack or spring ahead; at the long bound
We'll catch him. For the rest, my plan, thou know'st,
Though well matured, is not yet ripe; but sleep
Thou in security, and take thine ease,
For on thy brows the ∗∗∗ will soon be placed.
Enough, great captain; on thy steady sight,
Strong nerves, decisive movements, and true love,
My hopes and confidence are firmly built.
Hath the Fool Derrydown returned?
I know not.
I think he must ere this: let's to his house,
And we shall take him in's fine lace-edged sheets.

div.head: SCENE V.
div.stage: Poor People with fruit-barrows, baskets of cakes, nuts, fish, &c.

sp.speaker: Fishwoman.
sp.p: Any fish this morning, sir?— you'll find them very nice and fresh—this is all their nat'ral stiffness—no skewers run up along the back-bone: the real freshness of the gills—they hav'nt been washed with blood to redden 'em— these here eyes, what look so bright, are all their own—I doesn't do as some people do, goes and buys fish what are cheap in the market, and cuts out their fresh eyes to put into the ungodly heads of other stale fish what's expensive. Yah! keep your backy-smoke to yourself!

sp.speaker: Coalheaver.
sp.p: Don't you like smoke?

sp.speaker: Fishwoman.
sp.p: Not from sich as you.

sp.speaker: Coalheaver.
sp.p: What d'ye mean by that, you ugly old skate-faced psalm-singer?

sp.speaker: Several Voices.
sp.p: Go along with you all, you devil-gender'd set of cubs. Go and smoke Sal o'the barge.

div.stage: Enter two of the Masters Jaques, with slates and green bags, on their way to school.

sp.speaker: Eldest Boy
sp.p: A pen'orth o' nuts, please?

sp.speaker: Woman.
sp.p: Yes, I'll run and fetch the measure —I've lent it to a man close by—if you'll wait.

sp.speaker: Both Boys.
sp.p: Very well. Yes, we'll wait.

div.stage: Enter an Old Man with a small basket.

sp.speaker: Old Man
sp.p: Shrimps, gentlemen?

sp.speaker: A Coalheaver.
sp.p: Let's look at 'em, old chap?

sp.speaker: Old Man.
sp.p: They're werry fine, gentlemen.

sp.speaker: Coalheaver.
sp.p: Ben, you've got a ha'penny, and I've one; let's have a pen'orth a'tween us.

sp.speaker: Old Man.
sp.p: Yes, gentlemen, to be sure.

sp.speaker: Coalheaver.
sp.p: Come, heap up—good measure —there's your money, old cove.

sp.speaker: Old Man.
sp.p: Thank ye, gentlemen.

div.stage: Enter another Man with a basket.

sp.speaker: Man
sp.p: Any Chelsea buns, my rum-uns?

sp.speaker: Coalheaver
sp.p: Keep a civil tongue in your head ven you speaks to customers.

sp.speaker: Man.
sp.p: Well then, my coves?

sp.speaker: Coalheaver
sp.p: Who do you call coves!

sp.speaker: Man.
sp.p: Why, where's the harm?

sp.speaker: Coalheavers.
sp.p: We'll show you, you sarcy rascal!

sp.speaker: Woman.
sp.p: Here's the measure. A pint, did you say?

sp.speaker: Master Jaques.
sp.p: No, a pen'orth.

sp.speaker: 2nd Master Jaques.
sp.p: But are they real Barcelona ones?—not from our own woods?

sp.speaker: Policeman
sp.p: What, I've caught you all here again! Come along to the station-house. Be off, boys!

div.stage: (Pushes the youngest Master Jaques, who tumbles into the gutter.)

sp.speaker: 2nd Policeman.
sp.p: Come, you with the fish, and you with the basket of nuts, and you there with the fruit, and the rest of you—come away along with us directly.

sp.speaker: Master Jaques.
sp.p: What did you push my brother down for, you great brute?

sp.speaker: Policeman
sp.p: Hold your tongue. I'll sarve you the same.

sp.speaker: Master Jaques.
sp.p: What right have you to hit me? I am one of the sons of Mr. Jaques. He's got a crab stick at home!

sp.speaker: Policeman
sp.p: You and your brother shall come too.

sp.speaker: Fishwoman.
sp.p: You set of ungodly monsters, to take honest people to prison for no offence! I wish heaven may send down brimstone and fire upon you, and turn you all as black as coals!

div.stage: (They begin to drag her away, with several others).

sp.speaker: Fruitwoman.
sp.p: Oh, let me once get out of prison, this shall be a lesson to me! Oh, my poor children at home! 'Send I had but taken to thieving for you in time! I should not then have been dragged away to prison, there to reproach myself for being innocent against all reason!

sp.speaker: Old Man.
sp.p: I've done no harm! I've done no harm!

sp.speaker: Policeman.
sp.p: Come along, I say.

sp.speaker: A Woman.
sp.p: Oh the infamous magistrates of Babylon! that parish-bane, Mr. Blight! that pauper bully, Joskins! that mantrap, Mr. Diggary! that body without a heart, Mr. Hookem Walky,—he who told my starving sister and her child, that it was all cant and sham! What chance has honest indigence, when judged by wealthy knaves?

sp.speaker: A Coalheaver.
sp.p: She shows fight better than the old fish-fag. Don't hurt the woman.

div.head: SCENE VI.
div.stage: Enter Lord Busby and an Incendiary.

sp.speaker: Lord B.
sp.p: I heard you make the arrangements with your accomplice;—the fellow who is just turning round that low hedge yonder. It avails you nothing to deny the charge; it only adds more falsehoods to your life's long catalogue.

sp.speaker: Incen.
sp.p: I dare say if your catalogue, in that way, was measured, it wouldn't be a mere cat's-tail in length.

sp.speaker: Lord B.
sp.p: No doubt every man has his share to answer for, but do not forget the difference between one cat's-tail and nine!

sp.speaker: Incen.
sp.p: I didn't know who you were, when you first spoke; your present tender hint, however, refreshes my memory of your face, and tells me I am at the mercy of the great National Schoolmaster.

sp.speaker: Lord B.
sp.p: You are right; and mercy shall be shown, provided you do not persist in these outrages. Beware of the Schoolmaster!

sp.speaker: Incen.
sp.p: He ought to protect and justify me.

sp.speaker: Lord B.
sp.p: How so?

sp.speaker: Incen.
sp.p: He set me to the work!

sp.speaker: Lord B.
sp.p: What, to fire barns and hay-ricks!

sp.speaker: Incen.
sp.p: Or any thing else, that did mischief to monopolists' property.

sp.speaker: Lord B.
sp.p: Explain yourself, my man. How did the Schoolmaster teach you to do such things?

sp.speaker: Incen.
sp.p: He taught me to think.

sp.speaker: Lord B.
sp.p: Humph!—go on.

sp.speaker: Incen.
sp.p: He supplied me with cheap knowledge, such as I had never before dreamt of; and the novelty of learning histories of how the world had been governed all its life, in different countries; and how the people had always been treated; and how they sometimes resisted their tyrants, and played the very devil with their oppressors; made me think over these matters continually, and compare my own state and the state of Tempestorn, with others; and so I determined to follow good example, and play the devil with our oppressors here! Every one should exert his best efforts in the cause of thorough-going practical Reform. Some give arguments, who can get a hearing for them; others, who cannot argue, show their minds in action; and those who can argue, but can get no means of being heard, join hands with the latter. Thus a few administer the strong physic of reason and exhortation; the many let blood, blister, or cauterise. So you see, sir, what with one thing and another, the sheep-shearing conservatives are in a seasonable way of being silenced, tapped, fleeced in their turn, and finished.

sp.speaker: Lord B.
sp.p: You have nothing more to add, I presume?

sp.speaker: Incen.
sp.p: Nothing particular. For my own part, being among those whose reasons have no trumpeter, I am bound in duty to do my best, according to my own sphere of action; and so I contribute a little bit of incendiarism now and then, as often as I think my neck can safely afford it (for I'm not like a cat, who has as many lives as the tails you hinted at); and my donation may be considered as a sort of widow's mite, which I hope may prosper by stirring up the spirit of others in the same way.

sp.speaker: Lord B.
sp.p: This is candour, with a vengeance! Half a dozen hungry men like this, whose rude strong powers of thought and action are so sinuously balanced that each can equally support the other, or take its place and go alone, are enough to overturn any state in the world, in disturbed times.

So because you are given knowledge and taught to think, you set yourself to do all manner of mischief, by way of showing your gratitude? You might as well argue a right to commit murder, because the Creator had given you arms and strength!

sp.speaker: Incen.
sp.p: So I have, in self-preservation.

sp.speaker: Lord B.
sp.p: If any one offers you violence, you have the laws to fly to!

sp.speaker: Incen.
sp.p: The tax-gatherer and the parson offer me violence: they rob me of that which should procure me bread. Instead of my flying to the laws for protection, the laws fly at me, like bulldogs that my oppressors set on. Do you think I will work and be starved, to support great land-owners and fat monopolists of all ranks and classes? You have taught me too well.

sp.speaker: Lord B.
sp.p: You misapply the knowledge I have given you. You are young in thought, and must not act until you arrive at maturity.

sp.speaker: Incen.
sp.p: Teach me, then, a proper application; and please to begin by giving me work, and suffering me to keep enough of my earnings to live upon. I can't argue the question beyond this point; nor ought any man, if he could.

sp.speaker: Lord B.
sp.p: Would you have the blackamoor washed white in an hour? Would you have centuries of abuses ground young again and purified, as rapidly as imagination sees it done? Why should you, whose mind has only just learned to walk, endeavour to seize upon the horses of the sun, and begin to prove your ability by setting the world on fire?

sp.speaker: Incen.
sp.p: All this may be very fine, and quite true; but my truth, though in a vulgar corporal way, is as good as yours. I am willing to work: I must eat.

sp.speaker: Lord B.
sp.p: Well, well, of course, my man; there's no doubt of that. Here, take these five sovereigns, and go and get yourself some food and fresh clothes, for you appear to have seen better days. Depend upon it things will be rectified in due course, and the country will see prosperous times. Doubtless, you are acquainted with a great many men, who are pursuing the same mistaken line of conduct as yourself. Talk with them—reason with them— show them their error—and if you cannot dissuade them from these acts of violence, let me know who they are, and I will talk to them.

sp.speaker: Incen.
sp.p: Well, my lord, I thank you kindly for your advice; and I do admit I may have been in some error. There's nothing like talking to principals. I have learned more from your lordship in these five minutes, than from all the works that have issued from the press; whether really yours, or those of spurious schoolmasters. I'm sure I have no wish to lead an abandoned life, and I do begin to see that matters really are mending, and the country will soon be free and happy; and if, as your lordship recommends, I can persuade any of those misguided men to leave off their evil ways, I certainly will do so; and if they will not listen to reason, why then they must take the consequences.

sp.speaker: Lord B.
sp.p: Humph! good day, my friend; remember my injunctions. If you have a wife, go home to her.

sp.speaker: Incen.
sp.p: Most certainly, my lord; and God bless you, and thank you.

sp.speaker: Lord B.
sp.p: You are very welcome.

sp.speaker: Incen.
sp.p: This is the best day's work I've made this many a long year. How bright the sun shines on that hedge! it seems almost on fire. Is that a goldfinch I hear singing? No, it's a linnet. How pleasant the fields look, even at this time of the year!

div.head: SCENE VII.

sp.speaker: Policeman.
sp.p: Come, get up from that step, and march this way, along with the rest!

sp.speaker: A Man.
sp.p: We've been committing no offence!

sp.speaker: Policeman.
sp.p: What are you doing here?

sp.speaker: Several.
sp.p: Nothing; we're doing nothing!

sp.speaker: Policeman.
sp.p: Then I must take you all as vagrants.

sp.speaker: Several Voices.
sp.p: We've not been trying to sell anything; we have nothing to sell! And we have not been begging!

sp.speaker: Policeman.
sp.p: Are you quite sure of that? Didn't I see you begging a little while ago, in the other street?

sp.speaker: Several Voices.
sp.p: No, no, indeed, we have not; though we are quite destitute.

sp.speaker: Policeman.
sp.p: Destitute! come along!

sp.speaker: All.
sp.p: What for? what for?

sp.speaker: Policeman.
sp.p: You're quite destitute, that's enough for me; come along!

sp.speaker: A Man.
sp.p: I'll not be destitute again, when I once get out of prison!

div.stage: Sound of rough music outside. Enter Lord Slider, playing upon a pipe; Mr. Pullet with a tabor; and several M. P.'s, performing upon the tongs and the bones, leading on a Wedding Party, with morrisdance, &c.

lg.l: Oh, happy hour of jocund wedding!
The aspiring Tile-maker has caught her;
He reach'd her ere she gain'd the leading,
And won the Candle-maker's daughter!
Soap-boilers too, with spirit new,
Blacking and pill-puffers in papers,
Insurance brokers, laundress-soakers,
May inter-marry, and cut capers,
Divine Reform to them revealed,
Has taxes from their trades repealed.
Then glory to the great Reform,
Which noble Wigs have brought about:
The gallant pilots of the storm,
Who thus begin in proper form,
Nor heed the hungry rabble-shout.
For they have lighten'd thus our pains,
And very properly, I trow,
By doubling all our patriot gains,
Have taught their protegés to crow;
Cock-tailed a few with hot spiced porridge,
And left the tax on Corn and Knowledge.

div.head: SCENE VIII.
div.stage: A LONELY STREET OF EMPTY HOUSES.
Enter a Ruined Gentleman and his Wife.

lg.l: Nought more remains to try—I have tried all.
Early and late, since ruin swept our home
With less compunction than the moaning wind,—
Which hath the sound of pity, and although
It hath no heart, still seems a sufferer's echo—
Have I with indefatigable nerve,
Patiently toil'd. After unnumber'd throes
Of labouring hope and torture-wheel'd delay—
The heart's roots strain'd to the utmost, clasping thus
The birth and fate of each successive plan,
That with fresh life commenc'd, and prospects fresh,
But ended ever in the same dull corse,
With mutes or mourners round—aghast we stand
In hollow-eyed despair's exhaustion, fixed,
Like wrecks acute of consciousness, between
Necessity and impossibility.—
Recount not, love, the miseries of the past,
And all its harrowing trials; rather turn
This our last gaze upon those blissful bowers,
Embalm'd with our first love; there let us fix
Our thoughts, and in deep feelings drown farewell.
The pen, the pencil, language, voice, and harp,
We have tried all in vain; what else remained,
Except the spade?—and what its use's gain,
Unless I dig our graves? Being in distress,
And final pinch of want, it so falls out
That not one fraction of our utmost efforts
Turns to the least account: while, if no need
Oppressed us, not one fraction would be lost.
Gold rains on golden industry; but turns
To ashes, mockery, and sick despair,
Upon his head who struggles with Starvation!
Therefore—
Oh, reason not unto the end,
And wander round the outskirts of the deed
We have resolved to do; since it must be,
Why should we add the bitterness of thought
To all the countless preludes that have urged?
Our child is now in his third year.
Sweet love,
Speak not of him—I cannot bear that thought!
He must die too.
He must—we so agreed
Last night, when crying with the lack of food,
He could not sleep.
Soon will the infant sleep
In our stiff arms locked fast—a final rest.
This morn, we have resolved, shall be the last?
Fatepoints the way, having decreed it first.
Already do we feel the adder teeth
Of hunger, gnawing at life's inmost roots.
Would it were night-fall!
When the twilight haze
Obscures the vision's range across the park;
Thickens the trees into a general shade;
Confounds life's bodies with their peaceful trunks,
And hides (from such as might perchance pass by,
With eager pace to reach some happy home
Where waits a fond wife and the ready meal),
The harrowing cold expression of last looks
In those who seek their necessary graves—
We will escape this world! We've seen the poor
E'en now dragg'd savagely to suffer law,
Imprisonment, or stripes, or heavy toil,
For their atrocious destitution. Mark!
We are exposed to the same infamy,
And fully qualified. Spirit of life!
Treasure, as thou might'st be, still thou'rt worth nought,
When misery or disgrace poisons thy springs!
Let's haste to where we left our child asleep
In his exhaustion: to my bosom close
I'll hold him all the day, and at the hour
When moving tow'rds the watery shroud, prepared
By Providence for our extremity,
Our arms by turns shall press him to our hearts,
Until the moment when embracing close,
With him between, the welcome plunge we take.
Meantime, sweet love, o'ercome that darkening look—
Rack not thy sicken'd heart, now hope's no more;
And with meek dignity thus hand in hand,
Until the evening brings eternal rest,
We'll wander through this vacant, exiled world.

div.stage: (He places his hand upon her shoulder, and after gazing some time at her, kisses her.)

div.head: SCENE I.
div.stage: Enter King Anchorbroke in a laced Morning Gown.

sp.speaker: King Anchor.
sp.p: Things are in a pretty d---d state—all wrong a'tween decks, and far from right above board. I'm not sure but the magazine will be fired, and we shall all be blown to matches and tinder! The Quarter-deck nobles are now playing Tom Cox's traverse, and so are the mates and mids of the Main:—my precious soul! but I wish I could clap a tackle round some dozen picked specimens of both decks, and bring the bulls' noses down to the ring-bolts! How sharp the cat should sing in the air!—nothing like the thief's-cat for bringing rogues to their senses!
Don't like the aspect of things at all!
Weather black and squally overhead—hark! is that the Queen's voice—or the shrill whistle o' the wind?
Don't know, and I don't care—not much.
But what's all this?

I see in my haste to turn out, I've bent on her morning gown to my shoulders—here's a lot o' points and gim-cracks!— no matter, she often wears my canvass. Who's coming here so early?—old Bagnetlodge, I s'pose?

div.stage: Enter Earl Lovekin, who salutes his Majesty.

sp.speaker: King Anchor.
sp.p: Ah! Lovekin, my boy, how d'ye do to-day—how's your wife?

lg.l: Well, thank your Majesty; affairs of state
Prey not on ladies' constitutions.

sp.speaker: King Anchor.
sp.p: That's very true, Lovekin—I wish they did. But I'm afraid you're not very well yourself?

lg.l: I wait thus early on your Majesty,
In earnest hopes that—

sp.speaker: King Anchor.

lg.l: What can I do for you?

sp.stage: (laying his hand upon Earl Lovekin's shoulder.)

lg.l: Can I do any thing for you, or any of your family?
All are supplied; but I would pray your ear
To close attendance; for the nation now,
Like a vast whirlpool, threatens to engulf
Both throne and church in its own wild descent
To deep destruction. Therefore, your Majesty
Must now be firm—the crisis is at hand!
